title: Separating the LLM decision layer from driving in my Godot trucking sandbox
author: ViceGodIm
selftext:
For this experiment I kept navigation and physics in Godot and gave the model the business layer: jobs, route, driving pace, fuel stops and repayments. The input is structured state, without rendered frames.



That makes the trade-offs easier to inspect. A job can tie up cash, a faster route can cost more, and an inspection consumes shift time without adding revenue. I recorded the run so the visible outcome follows the selected actions.



My 4:13 edit: [https://youtu.be/ny6UgXJR96I](https://youtu.be/ny6UgXJR96I)



The challenge was to repay $6,000 and retain at least $1,200 cash.

comments.author: melty_program
comments.body: Does the decision layer get another turn if a chosen job becomes unaffordable after a fuel stop, or does Godot reject it and continue the current plan? That seems like an interesting test of the boundary: the explanation can sound sensible while the cash and time budget no longer supports it.

replies.author: ViceGodIm
replies.body:
It gets another turn after refuelling, with the updated cash and clock. Future jobs aren’t queued automatically. If it then picks a job it can’t cover the deposit for, the simulator rejects it and returns the error for one retry, without advancing time.

The catch is that passing that check doesn’t guarantee it can afford the whole trip or meet the deadline. It can still commit to a bad plan and suffer the consequences. That’s the gap I’d like to test more, a convincing explanation with numbers that don’t hold up.

replies.author: melty_program
replies.body: Thanks, that clears it up. Keeping the deposit check separate from the risk of a bad trip makes the distinction much clearer.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
For that gap I'd have the model write its own forecast into the action, like expected cash on arrival and expected arrival time, before the sim runs the trip. Then you can diff the forecast against what actually happened, and the convincing but wrong plans show up as a number instead of something you have to catch by rereading the explanation.



It also forces it to commit to arithmetic rather than just a reason. I'd keep the previous explanation text out of the next turn's context too, otherwise it can anchor on its own earlier justification.

replies.author: ViceGodIm
replies.body:
Yeah, I’d keep the forecast separate from validation, so a bad prediction still gets played out instead of being rejected. Then we could see whether it consistently underestimates travel time or forgets certain costs.

Good point about feeding its explanation back in, too. I’d return the actual outcome and forecast error on the next turn, without the old justification. That would make any correction much easier to measure. Thank you.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Letting the bad ones play out makes sense, you'd lose the pattern otherwise. Curious whether it actually adjusts once it sees its own forecast error, or keeps underestimating the same leg every time.
